structure.description: 18 books (parvans), traditionally 100 sub-books (upaparvans) as listed in the Parvasaṃgraha (1.2); the Harivaṃśa is its supplement (khila). The tradition speaks of 100,000 verses (śatasāhasrī saṃhitā); 1.1.61 says Vyāsa made a 24,000-verse Bhārata without the sub-stories (upākhyānas); 1.1.50 records three starting points used by reciters (Manu, Āstīka, Uparicara). summary: The great epic of the Bhārata war between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas, calling itself a 'fifth Veda' (kārṣṇa veda) and a treatise on dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa; besides the narrative it contains extended teaching sections (the Bhagavad Gītā, the Rājadharma, Āpaddharma and Mokṣadharma of the Śāntiparvan, the Anugītā, the Sanatsujātīya, Vidura's counsel, the Yakṣa's questions, the Nārāyaṇīya). It says of itself that what is found here on the four aims of life is found elsewhere, and what is not here is nowhere (1.56.33).

structure.description: 7 books (kāṇḍas). The poem itself speaks of 24,000 ślokas in 500 sargas, six books and the Uttara (1.4.2, vulgate). The local southern vulgate text has Bāla 77, Ayodhyā 119, Araṇya 75, Kiṣkindhā 67, Sundara 68, Yuddha 128, Uttara 111 sargas. The Baroda critical edition (1960–75) constitutes a shorter text.

summary: The first poem (ādikāvya): the life of Rāma, prince of Ayodhyā — his exile in obedience to his father's word, the abduction of Sītā by Rāvaṇa, the alliance with the monkeys and Hanumān, the war in Laṅkā, his righteous reign, and (in the last book) the banishment of Sītā. It presents Rāma as dharma embodied: truth to one's word, obedience to parents, fraternal loyalty, protection of those who seek refuge, and the king's duty to his subjects.
